intro: Long before there was a place called Illinois, there was a city. Around the year 1100, tens of thousands of people lived, farmed and traded at Cahokia, on the Mississippi River. They raised a mound of earth taller than a ten-story building. They built it one basket of dirt at a time. Cahokia was only one of hundreds of nations that lived across North America, each one shaped by its own land: forests, plains, deserts, coasts and ice.

Then, in 1492, ships crossed the Atlantic. What followed changed both sides of the ocean. Corn and potatoes fed Europe. Horses changed the Plains. Diseases killed more people than any war. Spanish soldiers, French traders and English farmers each treated the peoples they met differently. Native nations fought, made deals, adapted and survived.

In this unit you will learn how the land shaped Native ways of life, what the meeting of two worlds cost and carried, and how to read a source by asking who wrote it and why. You will end able to explain the same event from more than one point of view, using real evidence.
bigQuestion: How did the land shape the first peoples of North America, and how did meeting Europeans change both worlds?

timeline.t: People are living in North America; stone spear points and mammoth bones are the clues
Corn farming spreads across the Eastern Woodlands and the Mississippi valley
Cahokia in Illinois is at its peak, the largest city north of Mexico
Columbus reaches the Caribbean; the Columbian Exchange begins
Cortés and smallpox bring down the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan
English settle Jamestown and Plymouth; French settle Quebec in 1608
Marquette and Jolliet meet the Illinois people on the river
Metacom's war against the English in New England
The Pueblo Revolt drives the Spanish out of New Mexico
Pontiac unites Great Lakes nations against the British
The Black Hawk War and the Treaty of Chicago end Native landholding in Illinois
More than five hundred seventy Native nations are recognized; Chicago has a large Native community

words.d: an object made or used by people long ago, such as a spear point or pot
a large area where peoples shared similar foods, homes and tools because of the land
corn, beans and squash, planted together in one mound so each helps the others
bringing water to fields through ditches or canals
a hill made by people piling up earth, basket by basket
a group of nations that stay separate but join together to act on big decisions
having the right to govern itself with its own laws and leaders
the movement of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492
the body's ability to fight off a disease it has met before
a church and farm where priests required Native people to live, work and become Christians
a written agreement between a Native nation and a government, often about land
the position a person sees an event from, which shapes how they describe it

test.q: How do scientists know people lived in North America at least fifteen thousand years ago?
choices: From stone tools found with the bones of ice age animals
test.why: Spear points found with mammoth bones can be dated, and they show people were here long before any writing.

choices: Pueblos of mud brick in the Southwest
test.why: Southwest peoples built with stone and mud brick because there was little wood and the thick walls stayed cool.

test.q: Why did Plains peoples move during the year?
test.why: Their food, clothing and shelter came from bison, and the herds moved with the seasons.

test.q: What fed the city of Cahokia?
choices: Corn grown in the river bottom
test.why: Rich soil and corn farming let thousands of people live in one place.

test.q: What role did clan mothers play among the Haudenosaunee?
choices: They chose and could remove chiefs
test.why: The senior women of each clan picked the chiefs who sat on the Grand Council.

test.q: Copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf of Mexico at Cahokia show that
choices: trade routes stretched hundreds of miles
test.why: Neither item is found near Cahokia, so both had to arrive by long-distance trade.

test.q: Which is true of Native nations today?
choices: They are sovereign nations with their own governments
test.why: More than five hundred seventy nations are recognized, and many Native people live in cities like Chicago.

test.q: Why did Columbus sail west in 1492?
choices: To reach Asia and its spices by a new route
test.why: He believed Asia was a short sail west and that he could reach its trade goods directly.

test.q: Which pair shows the Columbian Exchange going in opposite directions?
choices: Corn to Europe and horses to the Americas
Wheat to Europe and cattle to the Americas
Potatoes to Europe and tomatoes to the Americas
Horses to Europe and pigs to the Americas
test.why: Corn was an American crop that went east, and horses were a European animal that came west.

test.q: Why did smallpox kill so many more Native people than Europeans?
choices: Native people lived in bigger cities
Native people had never met the germ and had no immunity
The disease was different in the Americas
test.why: Immunity comes from earlier exposure, and no one in the Americas had ever been exposed.

test.q: Which matches the country with how it usually treated Native peoples?
choices: Spain: traded furs and married in
England: built missions and forced labor
France: traded furs and made alliances
test.why: The few French who came depended on Native hunters, so they built alliances and trading posts.

test.q: Who led the 1680 uprising that drove the Spanish out of New Mexico?
test.why: Popé sent knotted cords to the pueblos so they would rise on the same day.

test.q: What did the Treaty of Chicago in 1833 do?
choices: Took the Potawatomi's last land in northern Illinois
test.why: After the treaty the Potawatomi were removed west, and almost no Native land was left in Illinois.

test.q: Learning to ride horses and to read treaties are examples of
test.why: Native nations took new tools and skills to protect themselves, which is adapting, not surrender.

test.q: Why should you ask who wrote a source and why?
choices: To find out if it is old
Because the writer's point of view shapes what the source says
Because only old sources are true
test.why: Columbus wrote to impress a king; Black Hawk spoke to explain a defeat. Purpose shapes every source.

write.prompt: Pick one Native nation or region from this unit. Make a claim about the biggest way meeting Europeans changed that nation's life. Support it with evidence from the readings, sources and data in the unit.
tips: Claim: state your answer in one sentence. Example: 'The horse changed Plains life more than anything else.'
Evidence: use at least two facts from the unit, such as a date, a number from a data table or a line from a source.
Reasoning: explain how each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just that it does.
The other side: name one different change someone could argue was bigger, and say why yours is stronger.
Point of view: say whose story your evidence comes from, and what the other side might add.
